run of entries shares a misunderstanding it helps to know they came from one hand in one season
rather than from everyone at once.

Volunteers new to cataloguing shadow an experienced hand for their first three boxes and are then
left to work alone, with the understanding that the first ten entries anyone writes will be read by
somebody else before they are filed. That reading is a conversation, not an inspection. Most of what
it catches is not error but habit: a tendency to guess at dates, to write scope notes as though the
reader already knew the family, or to let an interesting letter distract from the dull ledger that
actually tells the story of the box far better than the letter does. The habit is harmless in a reader
and expensive in a cataloguer. Neither is a fault in the person.

Pests and water are the two threats that arrive without warning. Sticky traps are checked monthly
and the count is written down, because a rising count is the only early signal of an infestation. The
water alarm under the strong room floor is tested on the first Saturday of each month, and the
person testing it signs the sheet on the door. An unsigned month is treated as an untested month,
whatever anyone remembers about it now.

Loans out of the building are rare and are approved only by the committee, in writing, for
exhibition by another archive or museum with its own strong room and its own insurance. A loan is
packed by two volunteers, photographed item by item before it leaves, and accompanied by a
condition report that the borrower countersigns on arrival. Nothing goes on loan to a private
individual, a shop window or a school display case, however worthy the occasion, because those are
the places from which things do not come back. The rule has been tested twice and has held both
times.

provenance.key:
The strong room is the only part of the building that is kept within a fixed range of temperature and
humidity, and it is the only place where catalogued material lives. Uncatalogued accessions wait in
the workroom on the metal shelving by the north wall. Nothing is stored on the floor, under a
window or on top of a radiator, however briefly, and the volunteer who finds a box in any of those
places moves it before doing anything else, including signing in or hanging up a coat.

Boxes are acid-free, lidded and of a single standard size, which means some collections are boxed
loosely and a few oversized items are boxed separately with a cross-reference. The standard size is
a deliberate constraint. Shelves are spaced for it, the trolley is built for it, and a volunteer can lift
any full box safely. A run of odd-sized boxes might save a little space and would cost us all three of
those things at once, and permanently, for every volunteer who follows.

Photographs are sleeved individually and stored on edge, not flat, in their own boxes. Negatives are
kept apart from prints. Anything on glass is boxed in padded trays and marked as such on the
outside, and glass is never carried more than one tray at a time. Newspaper cuttings are
photocopied onto archival paper and the copy is filed; the original is kept, but in a separate box,
because it will brown and embrittle whatever it touches, and given time it touches everything.

Handling rules are few and firmly kept. Hands are clean and dry; gloves are worn only for
photographs. Pencils only in the strong room and the reading room. Documents are supported on
the table or on a foam wedge, never held in the air. Bundles are untied and retied with the same
tape, and if the tape breaks it is replaced with unbleached cotton tape and the change is noted on
the box list. Nothing is ever fastened with a metal clip or a rubber band, and pins are unheard of.

The strong room log records every box that leaves the room and every box that returns, with the
time and the volunteer's initials. A box that is out for cataloguing may be out for weeks; that is fine,
provided the log says so. What the log prevents is the situation where a box is missing and nobody
can say whether it was ever on the shelf, was taken to the reading room, or went home in
somebody's bag by mistake, which has happened, exactly once, and was not found for a fortnight.
